![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14153452/assets/8901e7155a476f0019b6d66e3b62b579b91daf99a448e497c93efce1d94415b0.png)

Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨0,\,0,\,2x+yz⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by the bounding region of the rectangular solid shown above in the first octant. Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S.$
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that only the $z$-component of $F=⟨0,\,0,\,2x+yz⟩$ is non-zero. Since the lateral sides of $S$ are parallel to the $z$-axis, the flux of $F$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the top and bottom sides. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14153452/assets/8fa71e16d84eb92506e9b10269182f907cb4f2437d0a9bdd3822da48c4cbba4a.png)

 

Let's consider the flux of $F$ through these two sides.

- Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the top surface. On this surface, we have $z=2$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 1.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{1}$ is

$$
{n}_{1}=⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=2$ on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨0,\,0,\,2x+yz⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,2x+2y⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =2x+2y.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{1}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}{S}_{1} & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}2x+2y\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}2x+2y\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}2x+2y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[{x}^{2}+2xy]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}1+2y\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[y+{y}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

- Let ${S}_{2}$ denote the bottom surface. On this surface, we have $z=0$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 1.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{2}$ is

$$
{n}_{2}=⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=0$ on ${S}_{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{2} & =⟨0,\,0,\,2x+yz⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,2x⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =-2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}{S}_{2} & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}-2x\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}-2x\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}-2x\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}y{\int }_{0}^{1}2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-1\cdot {[{x}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-1\cdot 1 \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & =2+(-1) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14153452/assets/4cb2c8128f24adddacd82b5f477848faa47ae52f95a5bb0636a8b286a6628a08.png)

Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨0,\,0,\,{z}^{2}\sqrt{16-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by the bounding region of a right circular cylinder of height $2$ whose base is a circle of radius $2$ centered at the origin, as shown above. Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S.$
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that only the $z$-component of $F=⟨0,\,0,\,{z}^{2}\sqrt{16-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}⟩$ is non-zero. Since the lateral side of $S$ is parallel to the $z$-axis, the flux of $F$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the top and bottom sides. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14153452/assets/e6fe01196298c1da0961fd01c73ee4cb7c71b6a03a027cceaba0e68be944c968.png)

 
Let's consider the flux of $F$ through these two sides.

- Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the top surface. On this surface, we have $z=2$ for ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 4.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{1}$ is

$$
{n}_{1}=⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=2$ on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨0,\,0,\,{z}^{2}\sqrt{16-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,{2}^{2}\sqrt{16-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =4\sqrt{16-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{1}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}4\sqrt{16-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}S \\  & =4{∬}_{D}\sqrt{16-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying a change of variables $(x,y)\to (r,\theta ),\text{d}A=r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}4{∬}_{D}\sqrt{16-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & =4{∬}_{D}\sqrt{16-{r}^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2}r\sqrt{16-{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta {\int }_{0}^{2}r\sqrt{16-{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r \\  & =4\cdot 2\pi \cdot {\int }_{0}^{2}r\sqrt{16-{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r \\  & =8\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}r\sqrt{16-{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting $u=16-{r}^{2},$ we get $\text{d}u=-2r\,\text{d}r.$ Also, the limits must be changed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r & 0 & 2 \\ u & 16 & 12\end{aligned}
$$

 

Substituting these into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}8\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}r\sqrt{16-{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r & =8\pi \cdot {\int }_{16}^{12}\sqrt{u}(-\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u) \\  & =4\pi {\int }_{12}^{16}{u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =4\pi \cdot \frac{2}{3}{[{u}^{3/2}]}_{12}^{16} \\  & =\frac{8\pi }{3}[64-24\sqrt{3}] \\  & =\frac{64\pi (8-3\sqrt{3})}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Let ${S}_{2}$ denote the bottom surface. On this surface, we have $z=0$ for ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 4.$ Therefore, for everywhere on ${S}_{2},$ we have

$$
F(x,y,0)=⟨0,\,0,\,{0}^{2}\sqrt{16-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}⟩=⟨0,\,0,\,0⟩.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}0\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}0\,\text{d}S \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & =\frac{64\pi (8-3\sqrt{3})}{3}+0 \\  & =\frac{64\pi (8-3\sqrt{3})}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨0,\,0,\,x{y}^{2}+z⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by the bounding region of the rectangular solid shown above in the first octant. Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S.$
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that only the $z$-component of $F=⟨0,\,0,\,x{y}^{2}+z⟩$ is non-zero. Since the lateral sides of $S$ are parallel to the $z$-axis, the flux of $F$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the top and bottom sides. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14153452/assets/fa4986b1de44fa4ccc75114e64abfd93d0de16618f2f1b29695d9115019b6e3e.png)

 

Let's consider the flux of $F$ through these two sides.

- Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the top surface. On this surface, we have $z=4$ for $0\le x\le 2$ and $0\le y\le 1.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{1}$ is

$$
{n}_{1}=⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=4$ on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨0,\,0,\,x{y}^{2}+z⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,x{y}^{2}+4⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =x{y}^{2}+4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{1}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}x{y}^{2}+4\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}x{y}^{2}+4\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}x{y}^{2}+4\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+4x]}_{x=0}^{x=2}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2{y}^{2}+8\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{2}{3}{y}^{3}+8y]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{26}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Let ${S}_{2}$ denote the bottom surface. On this surface, we have $z=0$ for $0\le x\le 2$ and $0\le y\le 1.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{2}$ is

$$
{n}_{2}=⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=0$ on ${S}_{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{2} & =⟨0,\,0,\,x{y}^{2}+z⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,x{y}^{2}⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =-x{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}-x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & =-{∬}_{D}x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y{\int }_{0}^{2}x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{[\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}]}_{0}^{1}\cdot {[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\cdot 2 \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & =\frac{26}{3}+(-\frac{2}{3}) \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨0,\,0,\,{x}^{3}+{y}^{2}+z⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by the bounding region of the rectangular solid shown above in the first octant. Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S.$
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that only the $z$-component of $F=⟨0,\,0,\,{x}^{3}+{y}^{2}+z⟩$ is non-zero. Since the lateral sides of $S$ are parallel to the $z$-axis, the flux of $F$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the top and bottom sides. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14153452/assets/c058465d6ca7855446711ebc44f6b23913ee786d2fd9bb32ae6c671964e1ad32.png)

 

Let's consider the flux of $F$ through these two sides.

- Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the top surface. On this surface, we have $z=1$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 1.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{1}$ is

$$
{n}_{1}=⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=1$ on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨0,\,0,\,{x}^{3}+{y}^{2}+z⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,{x}^{3}+{y}^{2}+1⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & ={x}^{3}+{y}^{2}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{1}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}{x}^{3}+{y}^{2}+1\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{3}+{y}^{2}+1\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{3}+{y}^{2}+1\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}+x{y}^{2}+x]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}+\frac{5}{4}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}+\frac{5}{4}y]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{19}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Let ${S}_{2}$ denote the bottom surface. On this surface, we have $z=0$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 1.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{2}$ is

$$
{n}_{2}=⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=0$ on ${S}_{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{2} & =⟨0,\,0,\,{x}^{3}+{y}^{2}+z⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,{x}^{3}+{y}^{2}⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =-({x}^{3}+{y}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}-({x}^{3}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}S \\  & =-{∬}_{D}{x}^{3}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{3}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}+x{y}^{2}]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}+\frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{[\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}+\frac{1}{4}y]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{7}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & =\frac{19}{12}+(-\frac{7}{12}) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨0,\,xy-z,\,0⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by the bounding region of the rectangular solid shown above in the first octant. Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S.$
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that only the $y$-component of $F=⟨0,\,xy-z,\,0⟩$ is non-zero. Since the lateral sides of $S$ are parallel to the $y$-axis, the flux of $F$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the right and left sides. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14153452/assets/de9eb8381df05d2d5e6222a51b0ccbc5729e522df94a4aace570881d1226a1ca.png)

 

Let's consider the flux of $F$ through these two sides.

- Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the right surface. On this surface, we have $y=1$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le z\le 2.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{1}$ is

$$
{n}_{1}=⟨0,\,1,\,0⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $y=1$ on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨0,\,xy-z,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,1,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,x-z,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,1,\,0⟩ \\  & =x-z.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{1}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}x-z\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}x-z\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}x-z\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}-xz]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{2}-z\,\text{d}z \\  & ={[\frac{1}{2}z-\frac{1}{2}{z}^{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =1-2 \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

- Let ${S}_{2}$ denote the left surface. On this surface, we have $y=0$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le z\le 2.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{2}$ is

$$
{n}_{2}=⟨0,\,-1,\,0⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $y=0$ on ${S}_{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{2} & =⟨0,\,xy-z,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,-1,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,-z,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,-1,\,0⟩ \\  & =z.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}z\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}z\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}z\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}x{\int }_{0}^{2}z\,\text{d}z \\  & =[x]_{0}^{1}\cdot {[\frac{{z}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =1\cdot 2 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & =(-1)+2 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$
